description: Island kingdom in the western Mediterranean (1276–1343) created by the division of the Crown of Aragon among James I's sons; its strategic position on the Balearic archipelago made it a commercial intermediary between Italy and Iberia, but its economic dependence on Aragonese trade routes and military weakness before French and Aragonese pressure led to its absorption back into the Crown of Aragon.

temporal.notes: Aragonese cadet realm; Balearics and Roussillon.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Aragonese conquest of Majorca; cadet kingdom established 1276.
Kingdom stabilizes; Palma develops as western Mediterranean port.
Aragonese pressure; James III loses to Peter IV.

rise_factors.description: Majorcan merchants participated actively in western Mediterranean commerce linking Iberia, North Africa, and Italy.
James I of Aragon created a separate Majorcan kingdom for his second son, establishing a stable cadet branch.
Aragonese-Angevin alliance provided diplomatic backing for the independent Majorcan line.
James I of Aragon created the Kingdom of Majorca by bequest in 1262, giving his younger son control of the Balearic Islands and Roussillon as an independent appanage.
Majorca's central position in the western Mediterranean made it a critical waypoint for trade between Catalonia, Italy, and North Africa, with Palma becoming a prosperous commercial city.

decline_factors.description: James III's conflict with Peter IV of Aragon led to conquest of Majorca in 1343 and the kingdom's dissolution.
James III lacked the resources and allies to resist Aragonese military superiority.
Maintaining Montpellier and Roussillon as well as the Balearics stretched Majorcan resources beyond capacity.
Peter IV of Aragon conquered the Kingdom of Majorca in 1343–44, citing feudal violations to justify military annexation and reuniting the territories with the Aragonese crown.
France repeatedly pressured or occupied Roussillon and Montpellier, undermining the kingdom's continental territories and forcing constant diplomatic maneuvering that weakened the dynasty.
